evidence: Plaut. Mil. 46: Quanta istaec hominum summast?
terms.comment: Of a reckoning, the sum of all the items (Lewis & Short). To work out the total is summam subdūcere or summam facere; a total sum of money, summa pecūniae (Liv. 30.16.12, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Caes. BG 1.6: Erant omnīnō itinera duo
Cic. Clu. 76: quīnque omnīnō fuērunt (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 119: Omnīnō quattuor cubicula, four bedrooms in all

phrases.latin: Quanta istaec hominum summast? — Septem mīlia. — Tantum esse oportet. rēctē ratiōnem tenēs.
phrases.english: What’s the total number of men? — Seven thousand. — That’s what it should be; your sums are right.

phrases.latin: Erant omnīnō itinera duo, quibus itineribus domō exīre possent
phrases.english: there were only two routes in all by which they could leave home

phrases.latin: rēctē inquit Scaptius, sed subdūcāmus summam
phrases.english: ‘Fine,’ says Scaptius, ‘but let’s add up the total’

sources: Lewis & Short: summa · Lewis & Short: omnino
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 119, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).
Plautus (Mil. 46–47, Leo’s text), Caesar (BG 1.6) and Cicero (Att. 5.21.11) checked against the Perseus Latin texts.
